name: Whitening pens

lead: Whitening pens are pocket-sized applicators of peroxide gel that you paint onto the front teeth. People use them for quick touch-ups of shade between longer bleaching courses.

The gel releases free radicals that break down pigment molecules on and in the enamel, lightening stain over repeated use. Published work so far is laboratory testing on extracted teeth with several commercial pens; no human trials were found.

paras: Users paint the gel on clean, dry teeth, usually daily for a stretch of days or before an event. Home products like strips and trays are described as lightening about one or two shades, though the sources do not cover pens specifically.
Sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported effects of peroxide whitening. Lab studies have looked at peroxide passing into the pulp chamber and at enamel surface changes.

angle.text: Whitening pens paint peroxide gel onto the front teeth for quick touch-ups between longer bleaching courses, lightening stain over repeated use. Research so far is laboratory testing of branded pens.

lead: Whitening pens are over-the-counter applicator pens holding a peroxide-based gel that users paint onto the front of the teeth, mainly for touch-ups between longer bleaching courses. Colgate Optic White, Equate and Zimba-branded pens have been among those tested in laboratory work.[1][2]

Peroxide bleaching in general works by releasing free radicals that break pigment molecules into less coloured fragments.[3] Home products such as strips and trays are described as lightening teeth by about one or two shades, but the text reviewed does not cover pens specifically.[3]

Published human trials of whitening pens were not identified. Recent in vitro studies on extracted teeth have examined how much hydrogen peroxide reaches the pulp chamber, colour change and enamel surface changes with several commercial pens, with and without light activation or overnight use.[1][2][4]

paras: Pens deliver gel through a brush or felt tip and are applied for a set time, some designs overnight or paired with an LED light.[1][4]

Wikipedia describes sensitivity as the most common side effect of bleaching, and gum irritation or burns at higher peroxide concentrations.[3] Laboratory studies of pens focus on peroxide permeability into the pulp chamber and effects on enamel surface, reflecting these concerns.[2][4]

No studies found in humans. Laboratory studies on extracted premolars have compared commercial whitening pens for peroxide penetration into the pulp chamber, colour change and enamel surface morphology, including with light-activation systems and overnight use.[1][2][4]
